name: Oral probiotics (BLIS K12)
lead: Oral probiotics are live-bacteria products, typically lozenges, intended to colonize the mouth and throat. BLIS K12 is the best-known example in breath-focused discussion; it contains Streptococcus salivarius K12, a strain that produces bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances (BLIS).[1]

Wikipedia describes lozenges containing S. salivarius being sold to support defence against more virulent streptococci, and notes that some strains are being trialed to prevent oral infections.[1] The published evidence specifically for bad breath is limited, and an article on the strain itself covers the research in more detail.

paras: S. salivarius is an early colonizer of the mouth and upper airway and is usually harmless, though it is an opportunistic pathogen that rarely enters the bloodstream in people with neutropenia.[1] BLIS-producing strains can inhibit other bacteria, including Streptococcus pyogenes, the cause of strep throat.[1]

A registered randomized trial of 120 orthodontic patients examined the effect of oral probiotics on oral hygiene and halitosis; it is listed as completed, with no results summarized in the registry record.[2] A registered trial in nursery-age children examined S. salivarius K12 for preventing upper respiratory tract infection.[3] Many other widely cited oral-probiotic trials concern unrelated conditions and are not evidence for appearance uses.

card.summary: Probiotic lozenges built around S. salivarius K12, pitched for fresher breath; thin human evidence for that use.
card.note: Breath-specific trial data is sparse; see the S. salivarius K12 entry.

quick.overview:
Oral probiotics such as BLIS K12 lozenges are meant to seed the mouth with bacteria that compete with harmful ones. Breath-focused users take them hoping to reduce odor-producing species.

The breath-specific evidence is limited, with a few small or registered trials and no large published confirmation.
quick.mechanism: The K12 strain produces bacteriocin-like substances that can inhibit other bacteria, including strep throat bacteria.
quick.risks: S. salivarius is usually harmless but is a rare opportunistic pathogen in people with very low white blood cell counts.
